title: Harnessing Social Studies Instruction to Boost Literacy
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler surveys a cluster of new efforts to raise social studies out of its longstanding status as an under-resourced, marginalized elementary subject, anchoring the piece in a Fordham Institute finding that an extra half hour of daily social studies instruction is linked to higher fifth-grade reading scores, while an extra half hour of reading instruction is not. Because no national market exists for social studies curricula -- every state writes its own standards -- she highlights states building their own: Louisiana, Massachusetts, and now Kentucky, which is partnering with the Core Knowledge Foundation. The centerpiece of the piece is a site visit to Delaware's "Literacy for We the People" pilot, an $8.7 million federally funded program that trains teachers to use the Center for Civic Education's simulated-congressional-hearing model as a literacy vehicle, building on evidence that We the People already boosts civic knowledge 31% over controls. Wexler closes by noting the Four Question Method U.S. history curriculum's own call for social studies to have a "Sold a Story" reckoning, importing the evidence-based rigor that transformed reading instruction into history teaching.
points: A Thomas B. Fordham Institute study found that an extra half hour of daily elementary social studies instruction predicts higher fifth-grade reading scores, while an equivalent extra half hour of reading instruction does not -- evidence Wexler says supports building knowledge and vocabulary through content, not more test-prep-style reading skill drills.

Because every U.S. state writes its own social studies standards, no national curriculum market exists the way it does for literacy and math, pushing states like Louisiana, Massachusetts, and now Kentucky to build and give away their own curricula via partners like the Core Knowledge Foundation.

Delaware's federally funded "Literacy for We the People" pilot trains teachers to use simulated congressional hearings -- where student panels testify and field follow-up questions from judges -- as a vehicle for building writing, speaking, and civic knowledge simultaneously.

A CERL study of the underlying We the People program found it raised student civic knowledge 31% over a control group, with the largest gains among historically disadvantaged students, even as teachers report students retain little social studies content year to year without such reinforcement.
quotes: But six years ago, a study by the Thomas B. Fordham Institute turned up a surprising data point: when students spend an additional half hour per day on social studies in elementary school, their reading scores are higher by fifth grade. An extra half hour on reading, on the other hand, is not linked to higher reading scores.

The state department of education, in announcing the new curriculum, noted that "deep knowledge in civics, economics, geography and history strengthens students' reading comprehension, vocabulary, and academic language.

A key feature of the program is its culmination in a simulated congressional hearing. Panels of students present prepared statements on a particular topic to groups of judges, who then ask follow-up questions and provide feedback.

A study by CERL of the We the People program found it boosted students' civic knowledge by 31 percent as compared to a control group, with the strongest gains often among the historically disadvantaged.

I asked if their students seem to remember the social studies content they've had in previous years. They shook their heads wearily. One responded, "They don't even remember on Monday what they learned on Friday.

It's time, they wrote in a recent post, for the field of social studies to have its "Sold a Story" moment - following the lead of the "science of reading" movement in rejecting ineffective practices in favor of those grounded in the science of learning.
